05.01.title: Forces as vectors
05.01.html:
Statics begins with one idea: a force is a vector with a point of application. Get that right and everything else in this phase (moments, equilibrium, trusses, friction) is bookkeeping. Get it wrong and a scaffold that “adds up” on paper falls over. This lesson sets up the notation and the code you’ll reuse for the rest of the phase.

What a force is

A force has a magnitude (newtons), a direction and a line of action. In a rigid body you may slide a force along its line of action without changing its effect (the principle of transmissibility), but you may not move it sideways: that changes its turning effect, as the next lesson shows. So a force is a bound (or sliding) vector, unlike a free vector such as a displacement.

Components

In the plane, a force of magnitude F at angle θ to the x axis has components

Fx​=Fcosθ,Fy​=Fsinθ,F=Fx2​+Fy2​​,θ=atan2(Fy​,Fx​).

Use atan2, not atan: it gets the quadrant right. In 3D, a force of magnitude F along a cable from point A to point B is

F=F∣rB​−rA​∣rB​−rA​​,

the magnitude times a unit vector. That one formula handles every guy wire, cable and strut you’ll meet.

The resultant

Forces acting at one point (a concurrent system) combine into a single resultant, the vector sum:

R=i∑​Fi​,Rx​=∑Fx,i​,Ry​=∑Fy,i​.

Graphically, lay the arrows tip to tail; the resultant closes the polygon. If the polygon closes by itself, R=0 and the point is in equilibrium.

Worked exampleThree cables on a bamboo scaffold pole

Cables pull on a pole head with 2.0 kN at 30°, 3.0 kN at 135° and 1.5 kN at 250°.

  1. Components: (1.7321,1.0000), (−2.1213,2.1213) and (−0.5130,−1.4095) kN.
  2. Sum: Rx​=−0.9023 kN, Ry​=1.7118 kN.
  3. R=0.90232+1.71182​=1.9350 kN at atan2(1.7118,−0.9023)=117.79°.
  4. A fourth lashing of 1.9350 kN at −62.21° would balance the head exactly.

05.02.title: Moments and couples
05.02.html:
Push a door near its hinge and it barely moves; push at the handle and it swings. The turning effect of a force, its moment, depends on where it acts as much as on how big it is. Moments decide whether a crane tips, how much torque a bolt gets and how a bridge pier is loaded. This lesson defines the moment as a cross product, which works the same way in 2D and 3D.

The moment of a force about a point

For a force F acting at a point P, its moment about a point O is

MO​=r×F,r=rP​−rO​.

Its magnitude is ∣MO​∣=Fd, where d=rsinφ is the lever arm: the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action. That’s why sliding a force along its line of action changes nothing, and moving it sideways does. In the plane only the z component survives:

MO​=rx​Fy​−ry​Fx​(counter-clockwise positive).

Varignon’s theorem: the moment of a force equals the sum of the moments of its components. Split an awkward force into x and y parts and take each part’s moment separately.

Moment about an axis

In 3D, the turning effect about an axis through O with unit vector e is the projection Me​=e⋅(r×F). That’s the torque that actually turns a valve wheel or a shaft; the other components are carried by its bearings.

Couples

Two equal, opposite, parallel forces a distance d apart form a couple. They have zero resultant but a moment M=Fd, and that moment is the same about every point:

rA​×F+rB​×(−F)=(rA​−rB​)×F,

which doesn’t depend on the reference point. A couple is a free vector: a pure twist you can apply anywhere on the body. Your two hands on a steering wheel form one.

Worked exampleTightening a nut

A 120 N push at 70° to a 250 mm spanner handle.

  1. Components at the grip: Fx​=120cos70°=41.04 N along the handle, Fy​=120sin70°=112.76 N across it.
  2. Varignon: the component along the handle has zero lever arm, so M=0.25⋅112.76=28.19 N m.
  3. Lever arm d=M/F=234.9 mm, a little less than the handle length.
  4. A couple: two 50 N forces 0.4 m apart give 20 N m about every point. The code checks it about 20 random points.

Exercise 1Pedalling torque

A rider pushes straight down with 600 N on a 170 mm crank. What torque reaches the chainring when the crank is horizontal, and when it is 30° above horizontal?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Horizontal crank: the force is perpendicular to the crank, M=600⋅0.17=102 N m.
  2. At 30° above horizontal, the lever arm is the horizontal distance 0.17cos30°=0.1472 m, so M=88.3 N m.
  3. At top dead centre the lever arm is zero: pushing down does nothing, which is why riders “pedal in circles”.

05.03.title: Equivalent systems and distributed loads
05.03.html:
Real loads are messy: wind spread up a scaffold, people spread along a footbridge, soil pressing on a wall. For finding support reactions you can replace any load system with a much simpler one that has the same resultant force and the same moment about every point. This lesson shows how to make that swap and when it’s legitimate.

Force–couple systems

A force F at point A can be moved to any point B if you add a couple equal to the moment it had about B:

F at A≡F at B+MB​=rBA​×F.

Doing this for every force reduces any system to one resultant R=∑Fi​ at a chosen point plus one couple MO​=∑ri​×Fi​. Two systems are equivalent when both quantities agree. In the plane (and whenever R⊥MO​) you can go one step further: slide R sideways until its own moment equals MO​, and the couple disappears. For parallel loads along a beam, that line of action is

xˉ=∑Fi​∑xi​Fi​​.

Distributed loads

A line load q(x) (kN/m) is the continuous version of the same sum:

R=∫ab​q(x)dx,xˉ=R1​∫ab​xq(x)dx.

The resultant is the area under the load curve and it acts through the centroid of that area. Two shapes cover most cases: a uniform load q over L gives qL at mid-span, and a triangle rising to q gives qL/2 at L/3 from the high end. A trapezoid is a rectangle plus a triangle.

A warning. The equivalent load gives the right reactions for a rigid body. It doesn’t give the right internal forces or deflections: a beam carrying a spread load bends differently from one with a single point load. You’ll see the difference in lesson 05.13.

Worked exampleFootbridge deck and scaffold wind

  1. Trapezoid from 2 to 5 kN/m over 6 m: rectangle 2⋅6=12 kN at 3 m plus triangle 3⋅6/2=9 kN at 4 m. R=21 kN at xˉ=(12⋅3+9⋅4)/21=3.4286 m.
  2. Wind on a 12 m scaffold, q=0.9(z/12)2/7 kN/m: R=0.9⋅12⋅97​=8.4 kN acting 169​⋅12=6.75 m up. The code gets both by Simpson’s rule.

Exercise 1Four point loads

A beam carries 10 kN at 1 m, 4 kN at 2.5 m, an uplift of 3 kN at 4 m and 8 kN at 5 m. Reduce this to a force and couple at x=0, then to a single force.

  2. M0​=10⋅1+4⋅2.5−3⋅4+8⋅5=48 kN m.
  3. Single force: xˉ=48/19=2.5263 m. Any support calculation gives the same reactions with this one force as with the four.

05.04.title: Rigid body kinematics in the plane
05.04.html:
Statics deals with bodies at rest, but you need to describe how a rigid body can move before you can stop it moving. Supports remove possible motions, mechanisms keep some of them, and the virtual work method in lesson 05.19 is built entirely on small rigid motions. This lesson gives the one formula that describes every planar rigid motion.

Rigid motion

A body is rigid if the distance between any two of its points never changes. In the plane, its position has three numbers: two for a reference point and one for an angle. Those are its three degrees of freedom. Its velocity is also three numbers: the velocity vA​ of one point A and an angular velocity ω (counter-clockwise positive). Every other point follows from

vB​=vA​+ω×rAB​,ω×r=ω(−ry​,rx​).

The relative velocity of B with respect to A is perpendicular to AB, with magnitude ω∣AB∣. A rigid body can’t stretch, so no relative velocity along AB is possible.

The instantaneous centre

If ω=0, there is exactly one point (perhaps off the body) whose velocity is zero right now:

rI​=rA​+ωk^×vA​​.

At that instant the body is purely rotating about I: every point moves perpendicular to its line to I with speed ∣ω∣dI​. To find I by drawing, draw perpendiculars to the known velocity directions of two points; they cross at I. For a wheel rolling without slip, I is the contact point, so the top of the wheel moves at twice the hub speed.

Worked exampleBicycle wheel and engine slider-crank

  1. Wheel, r=0.35 m, hub at 8 m/s: ω=−8/0.35=−22.86 rad/s. The top point moves at 8+22.86⋅0.35=16 m/s, the front point at (8,−8) m/s, the contact point at zero.
  2. Slider-crank, r=50 mm, l=200 mm, crank at 60° turning at 100 rad/s: crank pin A=(0.025,0.0433) m, vA​=(−4.330,2.5) m/s. Piston B=(0.2203,0).
  3. B moves only horizontally, so vB,y​=0=2.5+ωrod​(0.2203−0.025), giving ωrod​=−12.80 rad/s.
  4. vB​=−4.330−(−12.80)(−0.0433)=−4.885 m/s. The rod’s instantaneous centre is at (0.2203,0.3815) m, and ∣vB​∣=12.80⋅0.3815. The code also checks vB​ by differentiating the piston position numerically.

Exercise 1Crank at 90°

Same slider-crank, crank at 90°. Find the rod’s angular velocity and the piston velocity. Where is the instantaneous centre?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A=(0,0.05), vA​=100⋅(−0.05,0)=(−5,0) m/s, horizontal.
  2. B also moves horizontally, so both velocities are parallel. Their perpendiculars are parallel too and never meet: the instantaneous centre is at infinity.
  3. The rod is translating at this instant: ωrod​=0 and vB​=−5 m/s, the same as the crank pin. That’s close to the piston’s peak speed.

05.05.title: Supports, constraints and degrees of freedom
05.05.html:
A bridge girder sits on a pin at one end and a roller at the other, not on two pins. A motorbike’s rear suspension is a linkage with exactly one way to move. Both choices come from counting freedoms and constraints. Before you write any equilibrium equation, you should know whether the body can be held still by its supports, and whether the supports fight each other. That’s what this lesson is about.

Idealised supports

Each planar support stops some motions and supplies one reaction component for each motion it stops:

Support Prevents Reactions
Roller (or link, smooth surface) motion normal to the surface 1 force, normal to the surface
Pin (hinge) both translations 2 force components
Clamp (fixed, built-in) translations and rotation 2 forces and 1 moment
Cable motion away from the anchor 1 tension, along the cable, pulling only

A real support is somewhere in between: a bolted connection is partly fixed, a bearing pad resists sliding a little. Choosing the idealisation is part of the modelling.

Counting

A free rigid body in the plane has 3 degrees of freedom. With r reaction components the count is

DOF=3−r.
  • r<3: a mechanism; the body can move.
  • r=3 and the reactions are properly arranged: statically determinate; the three equilibrium equations give all reactions.
  • r>3: statically indeterminate; there are more unknowns than equations, and you need deformation (Phase 06) to solve.

That’s why bridges use a pin and a roller: three reactions, and the roller lets the girder expand with temperature without building up force.

Counting is not enough: the rank

Three reactions can still fail. Three vertical rollers have r=3 but nothing resists horizontal sliding. A pin plus a roller whose reaction line passes through the pin can’t resist rotation about that pin. Write each unit reaction as a row (Fx​,Fy​,MO​); the supports work only if this matrix has rank 3. A rank below 3 is called improper (or geometric) instability, and it’s a classic exam trap and a classic real failure.

Linkages: Grübler’s formula

For n links (counting the ground) joined by j1​ pins or sliders (each removing 2 freedoms) and j2​ rolling or cam contacts (each removing 1):

M=3(n−1)−2j1​−j2​.

A four-bar linkage has M=3⋅3−2⋅4=1: one input drives the whole thing. A triangle of three bars has M=0, which is why trusses are made of triangles.

Worked exampleA footbridge and some linkages

  1. Pin at the left end, roller at the right: r=3, DOF =0, rank 3: determinate.
  2. Pin at both ends: r=4, DOF =−1: one degree indeterminate. Heating the girder would build up axial force.
  3. Three vertical rollers: r=3 but rank 2: a mechanism that slides sideways.
  4. Grübler: four-bar 1, slider-crank 1 (the slider counts as a joint), five-bar 2, triangle 0, Stephenson six-bar with 6 links and 7 joints gives 1.

Exercise 1A motorbike rear suspension

The swingarm is pinned to the frame. A rocker is pinned to the frame, a link joins the rocker to the swingarm, and the shock absorber (modelled as a rigid link for now) joins the rocker to the frame. How many links and pins, and what is the mobility? What happens when the shock is allowed to change length?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Links: frame (ground), swingarm, rocker, link, shock: n=5. With the shock rigid, joints: swingarm–frame, rocker–frame, link–rocker, link–swingarm, shock–rocker, shock–frame: j1​=6.
  2. M=3⋅4−2⋅6=0: a rigid structure.
  3. Letting the shock slide (its two halves become two links joined by a slider) adds one link and one joint: M=3⋅5−2⋅7=1. The wheel has exactly one way to move, and the shock controls it.

05.06.title: The free-body diagram
05.06.html:
Almost every statics mistake happens before the first equation: a forgotten force, a reaction in the wrong direction, an internal force counted twice. The free-body diagram (FBD) is the tool that prevents this. It is the most important drawing in mechanical engineering, and the habit carries straight into dynamics, machine design and finite elements.

The cut principle

Cut the body free from everything that touches it, then replace each contact with the force (or couple) it can transmit. What remains is the body alone, with

  • applied loads: weights, people, wind, pressure;
  • reactions at every cut support, with as many components as the support can carry (lesson 05.05);
  • nothing else. Forces inside the body cancel in pairs (Newton’s third law) and don’t appear.

If you cut through a body instead of around it, the cut exposes internal forces, equal and opposite on the two sides. That’s how you’ll find forces in truss members (05.09) and bending moments in beams (05.13).

Rules that prevent mistakes

  1. Draw the body alone, then draw every force at its true point of application.
  2. For unknown reactions, assume a direction and label it. A negative answer just means the arrow points the other way; never redraw it mid-solution.
  3. Friction acts along the contact surface and opposes the motion that would happen. A smooth surface has a normal force only.
  4. Use consistent units and a sign convention (counter-clockwise positive here).

In the plane, the FBD gives exactly three independent equations:

∑Fx​=0,∑Fy​=0,∑MO​=0.

Once the forces balance, the moment sum is the same about every point, so you may pick O wherever it kills the most unknowns.

Worked exampleThe ladder FBD

Ladder 5 m long at 65°, ladder weight 200 N at mid-length, person 800 N at 3.75 m up. The wall is smooth.

  1. Unknowns: wall push Nw​ (horizontal), floor normal Nf​, floor friction Ff​.
  2. ∑Fy​=0: Nf​=200+800=1000 N.
  3. ∑M about the foot (kills Nf​ and Ff​): Nw​⋅5sin65°=200⋅2.5cos65°+800⋅3.75cos65°, so Nw​=326.42 N.
  4. ∑Fx​=0: Ff​=Nw​=326.42 N, towards the wall. The floor needs μ≥326.42/1000=0.3264.
  5. The code checks the residual is zero about three different points, and shows the check catching an FBD with the friction left out.

Exercise 1How high is safe?

Same ladder and person, but the floor only offers μ=0.25. How far up the ladder can the person go before it slips?

  1. Limit: Ff​=μNf​=0.25⋅1000=250 N, so Nw​=250 N.
  2. Moments about the foot: 250⋅5sin65°=200⋅2.5cos65°+800scos65°.
  3. 1132.9=211.3+338.1s, so s=2.726 m: a bit over halfway. Above that, the ladder slides out. Steeper ladders or a rubber foot help.

05.07.title: Equilibrium of rigid bodies
05.07.html:
With a clean free-body diagram, equilibrium is three equations in the plane and six in space. This lesson turns them into a solver for beams with any mix of point loads, distributed loads and couples. It also shows a 3D case, a hung platform, where the same idea gives three useful equations out of six.

The equations

A rigid body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant moment both vanish:

∑F=0,∑MO​=0.

In the plane that is ∑Fx​=∑Fy​=∑MO​=0. You can swap a force equation for a second moment equation about a different point, as long as the line between the two points isn’t perpendicular to the remaining force direction. Picking moment points at unknown reactions is the classic trick: each moment equation then has only one unknown.

Beams

For a beam on a pin at a and a roller at b, with vertical loads only, the horizontal pin reaction is zero and

Rb​=b−a∑Pi​(xi​−a)−∑Mj​​,Ra​=∑Pi​−Rb​,

with distributed loads replaced by their resultants (05.03) and couples Mj​ counter-clockwise positive. Check the answer with a moment equation about the other support: if it doesn’t balance, something is wrong.

In 3D

A body in space has six equations: three forces, three moments. Special load cases need fewer. A horizontal platform hung from vertical cables only has ∑Fz​, ∑Mx​ and ∑My​ left; the other three are automatically zero. So three cables are determinate, and a fourth would be one too many.

Worked exampleOverhanging footbridge beam

Pin at 0, roller at 6 m, beam to 8 m. Loads: 20 kN at 2 m, 5 kN/m over 0 to 6 m, 10 kN at the tip.

  1. The UDL becomes 30 kN at 3 m.
  2. ∑MA​=0: 6Rb​=20⋅2+30⋅3+10⋅8=210, so Rb​=35 kN.
  3. ∑Fy​=0: Ra​=20+30+10−35=25 kN.
  4. Check, moments about B: −25⋅6+20⋅4+30⋅3−10⋅2=0. Correct.
  5. A lone 15 kN m couple on a 5 m span gives Ra​=3 kN up and Rb​=3 kN down, wherever the couple sits.

Exercise 1A stage platform on three cables

A 2 m × 1.2 m platform hangs from cables at (0,0), (2,0) and (1,1.2) m. It carries 3 kN at its centre (1,0.6) and 1.5 kN of equipment at (1.6,0.3). Find the cable tensions.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ∑Fz​: T1​+T2​+T3​=4.5.
  2. ∑Mx​ (moments of y): 1.2T3​=3⋅0.6+1.5⋅0.3=2.25, so T3​=1.875 kN.
  3. ∑My​ (moments of x): 2T2​+1⋅T3​=3⋅1+1.5⋅1.6=5.4, so T2​=1.7625 kN.
  4. T1​=4.5−1.875−1.7625=0.8625 kN. All positive, so no cable goes slack.

05.08.title: Static determinacy
05.08.html:
Some structures can be solved with statics alone; others need you to know how they deform. Telling them apart before you start saves hours, and it matters in design too. A determinate bridge doesn’t care if a support settles or the sun heats it. An indeterminate one builds up internal force when that happens, but it also has a spare load path if a member fails.

Equations against unknowns

Split a structure into b rigid bodies joined by internal hinges. Each body gives 3 equations, so there are 3b equations. The unknowns are the r support reactions plus 2 forces at every internal hinge. Write all the equations as a matrix system Ax=f, where each column of A is one unknown’s contribution to the forces and moments on each body. Then

free motions=3b−rankA,degree of indeterminacy=nunknowns​−rankA.
  • Both zero: statically determinate. One unique solution for any load.
  • Free motions >0: a mechanism. Some loads can’t be balanced at all.
  • Indeterminacy >0: statically indeterminate. Equilibrium allows infinitely many solutions; the deformation picks one.

A structure can be both a mechanism and indeterminate at once: rigid in one direction with spare supports, free in another. Counting alone (n against 3b) can’t see that. The rank can.

Classic cases

Structure Bodies Unknowns Verdict
Pin + roller 1 3 determinate
Clamp + roller (propped cantilever) 1 4 1× indeterminate
Clamp + clamp 1 6 3× indeterminate
Clamp, hinge, roller (Gerber beam) 2 6 determinate
Three-hinged arch 2 6 determinate
Pin, hinge, roller 2 5 mechanism

Adding a hinge to a beam releases one internal moment, so it takes away one degree of indeterminacy. Heinrich Gerber used exactly that in the 1860s to make long continuous bridges determinate: a hinge per extra support. Many Swiss road bridges are continuous girders made the other way, indeterminate on purpose for stiffness and redundancy.

Worked exampleClassifying by rank

  1. Propped cantilever: unknowns 4, equations 3, rank 3. Indeterminacy 4−3=1.
  2. Gerber beam: clamp (3) + hinge (2) + roller (1) = 6 unknowns, two bodies give 6 equations, rank 6: determinate.
  3. Pin at the left, roller at the right but rolling horizontally, in line with the pin: rank 2. One free motion (rotation about the pin) and one redundant reaction (two horizontal reactions on one line).

Exercise 1A three-span bridge

A continuous girder has a pin at the left end and rollers at three more piers (4 supports in total, no hinges). How indeterminate is it? How many hinges, and where, would make it determinate without making it a mechanism?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Unknowns 2+1+1+1=5, equations 3, rank 3: 2× indeterminate.
  2. Each hinge adds a body (3 equations) and 2 unknowns, so it removes one degree. Two hinges make it determinate.
  3. Put them in different spans, never two in one span. A sensible choice is one hinge in each outer span, near the inner piers, so the middle span becomes a beam with two cantilevers that carry suspended end pieces. Two hinges in one span would leave that piece with no support of its own: a mechanism even though the count is right.

05.09.title: Plane trusses and the method of joints
05.09.html:
Look at an old railway bridge, a roof over a sports hall or a crane boom and you’ll see triangles. A truss is a set of straight bars joined at their ends so that every bar only pulls or pushes along its own axis. That makes trusses light, stiff and easy to analyse. This lesson builds a solver that handles any plane truss and shows what happens when you remove a member.

Two-force members

An ideal truss assumes pinned joints, loads only at joints and weightless bars. Each bar then has forces at its two ends only, and equilibrium forces them to be equal, opposite and along the bar. One number per bar describes it: the axial force N, positive in tension.

The method of joints

Every joint is a particle, so it gives two equations, ∑Fx​=∑Fy​=0. A bar from joint i to joint j with unit vector eij​ pulls joint i with Neij​ when in tension. With j joints, m bars and r reactions,

2j=m+r

is the counting condition for a determinate truss (and the rank must also be full). Built from triangles, a simple truss has m=2j−3 bars, which with 3 reactions is exactly right. By hand you start at a joint with only two unknowns and walk across the truss. By computer you assemble all 2j equations and solve them at once.

Zero-force members are worth spotting by eye. At an unloaded joint where two bars are collinear and a third isn’t, the third carries nothing. They aren’t useless: they brace long compression bars against buckling and carry other load cases.

Worked exampleA three-panel Warren truss

Equilateral triangles with 4 m sides, pin at joint 0, roller at joint 3, 10 kN at each of the two inner bottom joints. 7 joints, 11 bars, 3 reactions: 14=11+3.

  1. By symmetry, both reactions are 10 kN up.
  2. Joint 0: the diagonal 0–4 at 60° has Nsin60°+10=0, so N04​=−11.547 kN (compression).
  3. N01​+N04​cos60°=0, so N01​=5.774 kN (tension).
  4. The full solve also gives the middle bottom chord at 11.547 kN tension, the top chord at 11.547 kN compression, and zero force in the two middle diagonals: with symmetric loads, no shear crosses the middle panel.
  5. Delete diagonal 4–1 and the joint equations become singular: a mechanism.

  2. ∑Fy​: N14​sin60°+N15​sin60°−10=0.
  3. ∑Fx​: −5.774+11.547−0.5N14​+0.5N15​=0.
  4. From these, N14​+N15​=11.547 and N14​−N15​=11.547, so N14​=11.547 kN (tension) and N15​=0. That matches the solver.

05.10.title: The method of sections
05.10.html:
The method of joints gives every bar force, but often you only need one: the most loaded chord, or the bar a crack was found in. The method of sections gets a single bar force in one equation by cutting the truss in two and balancing one side. Inspectors and designers use it daily.

Cutting a truss

Cut through the truss along a line that crosses (usually) three bars, not all meeting at one point. Take one part as a free body. Its loads are the external loads and reactions on that side, plus the three unknown bar forces, drawn as tension pulling away from the part. Three equations, three unknowns.

The trick is to choose the equations well:

  • For a chord force, take moments about the joint where the other two cut bars meet. Only one unknown is left.
  • For a diagonal between parallel chords, use ∑Fy​: the horizontal chords drop out.

Why the chord forces grow towards mid-span

Take moments for a bottom chord force Nb​ about the top joint above it. The left part’s loads give exactly the bending moment M(x) that a beam would have there, and Nb​ has lever arm h:

Nb​=hM(x)​.

So a truss is a beam whose chords carry the bending moment as a tension–compression pair, and whose diagonals carry the shear. That’s why chords are heaviest at mid-span, diagonals are heaviest near the supports, and a deeper truss needs lighter chords.

Worked examplePanel 3 of a Pratt bridge

Six 3 m panels, height 4 m, 12 kN at each of the 5 inner bottom joints. Reactions are 30 kN each. Cut panel 3, between x=6 and 9 m: top chord T2–T3, diagonal T2–B3, bottom chord B2–B3. Left part: reaction 30 kN at 0, loads 12 kN at 3 and 6 m.

  1. Bottom chord, moments about T2 at (6,4): 4Nb​=30⋅6−12⋅3, so Nb​=36 kN (tension).
  2. Top chord, moments about B3 at (9,0): −4Nt​=30⋅9−12⋅6−12⋅3, so Nt​=−40.5 kN (compression).
  3. Diagonal (slope 3:4, so its vertical share is 0.8): 30−12−12−0.8Nd​=0, so Nd​=7.5 kN (tension).
  4. The code matches all three against a full method-of-joints solve.

Exercise 1Panel 2

Same bridge. Cut panel 2 (3<x<6 m) and find the bottom chord B1–B2 and the diagonal T1–B2.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The cut crosses T1–T2, T1–B2 and B1–B2. Left part: reaction 30 kN at 0, load 12 kN at 3 m.
  2. Bottom chord, moments about T1 at (3,4): 4Nb​=30⋅3, so Nb​=22.5 kN.
  3. Diagonal: 30−12−0.8Nd​=0, so Nd​=22.5 kN tension, three times the panel 3 diagonal. Shear is larger near the supports.

05.11.title: Space trusses and towers
05.11.html:
Ski-lift pylons, electricity towers and stage rigs are space trusses: bars in three dimensions, pinned at the joints. Everything from plane trusses carries over with one more equation per joint. What changes is that 3D instability is much harder to see by eye, so the rank check from 05.08 becomes essential.

Joints in space

Each joint is a particle in 3D, so it gives three equations, ∑Fx​=∑Fy​=∑Fz​=0. A bar from i to j pulls joint i with Neij​, where

eij​=∣rj​−ri​∣rj​−ri​​.

A ball-and-socket support gives 3 reactions, a slot or roller fewer. Maxwell’s rule for a determinate space truss is

m+r=3j,or m=3j−6 for a free-standing truss held by 6 reactions.

The simplest rigid space truss is a tetrahedron: 4 joints, 6 bars, 6=3⋅4−6. Keep adding a joint with 3 bars to existing joints and the truss stays rigid. That’s how tower designers think: triangulate every face.

Necessary, not sufficient

Maxwell’s count can be satisfied while the truss still moves. Put two braces in one face of a tower and none in the next: the count is unchanged, but the unbraced face is a parallelogram that can shear. Only the rank of the 3j×(m+r) equilibrium matrix tells you for sure.

Worked exampleA tripod and a pylon

  1. Tripod: apex 4 m above three feet on a circle of radius 1.5 m, 12 kN down at the apex. Each leg is L=1.52+42​=4.272 m long. By symmetry the vertical components share the load: 3N⋅4/4.272=−12, so N=−4.272 kN in each leg.
  2. Add a 3 kN sideways pull and one leg goes into tension (1.424 kN) while the other two carry −7.12 kN.
  3. Pylon with rope load 5 kN at each top joint and 3 kN of wind at two of them: m+r=12+12=24=3⋅8, rank 24, determinate. The windward diagonal carries −18.6 kN and one leg goes into 13.1 kN tension.
  4. Brace one side twice and leave the front face open: still 24=24, but rank 23. A mechanism.

Exercise 1Counting a lattice mast

A three-legged lattice mast has 10 levels of joints above its base (3 joints per level, 33 joints including the 3 base joints, all base joints pinned). Each level adds 3 horizontal bars, 3 leg segments and 3 face diagonals. Is Maxwell’s count satisfied?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Free joints: 30, each with 3 equations: 90 equations for those joints. The pinned base joints add 9 equations and 9 reactions, which balance each other.
  2. Bars: 10 levels × 9 = 90.
  3. 90=90: the count is right. Every face is a triangle, so the rank is full too. That’s exactly how lattice masts are built.

05.12.title: Frames and machines
05.12.html:
Pliers, bike brakes, excavator arms and car suspensions are not trusses: their members are bent or carry loads along their length, so member forces aren’t along the members. These are frames (built to stand still) and machines (built to transmit force). You analyse them by taking them apart and drawing an FBD of each piece.

Taking a frame apart

  1. Look at the whole structure first. Its FBD often gives some support reactions directly.
  2. Separate the members at their pins. At each internal pin, draw the force pair as two unknown components, equal and opposite on the two members (Newton’s third law).
  3. Spot any two-force members (straight or not, loaded only at two pins). Their force is along the line joining the pins, which saves an unknown.
  4. Write three equations per member and solve.

A cable or chain between two bodies acts the same way: one tension, pulling both ends.

Mechanical advantage

A machine turns an input force into a larger (or faster) output. For a lever pivoted at O with input Fin​ at distance a and output at distance b, moments about O give

Fout​=Fin​ba​.

Chain several levers and the advantages multiply. Energy is conserved, though: the output moves a/b times less. That trade appears again in the virtual work method (05.19).

Worked exampleA bicycle rim brake

Finger force 60 N at 70 mm from the lever pivot; cable anchor 25 mm from the pivot. On the caliper, the cable pulls 100 mm from the arm pivot; the pad sits 40 mm from it.

  1. Lever, moments about its pivot: T⋅25=60⋅70, so T=168 N. The pivot carries 168−60=108 N.
  2. Arm, moments about its pivot: N⋅40=168⋅100, so N=420 N. Its pivot carries 420−168=252 N.
  3. Overall: 420/60=7=(70/25)(100/40).
  4. Two pads with μ=0.6 give 2⋅0.6⋅420=504 N of friction on the rim.
  5. If the cable pulls 20° off perpendicular, its lever arm shrinks by cos20° and the tension rises to 178.8 N for the same squeeze.

Exercise 1Pliers

Pliers have handles 110 mm long from the pivot and jaws 22 mm from the pivot. You squeeze each handle with 150 N at its end. What is the gripping force, and what force does the pivot pin carry?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. One half of the pliers, moments about the pin: Fjaw​⋅22=150⋅110, so Fjaw​=750 N.
  2. Force balance on that half (the hand and jaw forces are parallel): the pin carries 750+150=900 N.
  3. Mechanical advantage 5. The pin carries more than either the grip or the squeeze, which is why it is the part that wears.

05.13.title: Internal forces in beams
05.13.html:
Reactions tell you what the supports feel. To size a beam you need what the beam feels inside: at every section, how hard it is being sheared and bent. Those internal forces, plotted along the beam, are the shear force and bending moment diagrams. Every beam, shaft, floor joist and crane boom is designed from them.

Cutting a beam

Cut the beam at position x and look at the left part. To keep it in equilibrium, the right part must act on it with

  • an axial force N(x) along the beam,
  • a shear force V(x) across it,
  • a bending moment M(x).

With the usual sign convention (positive M sags the beam, bottom in tension), equilibrium of the left part gives V as the sum of the upward forces to the left, and M as the sum of their moments about the cut.

The differential relations

Balance a short slice dx carrying a distributed load q (downward positive):

dxdV​=−q,dxdM​=V.

These two lines are the whole method:

  • With no distributed load, V is constant and M is linear between point loads.
  • Under a uniform load, V is linear and M is a parabola.
  • A point load makes V jump by its size; M gets a kink.
  • M is largest where V crosses zero.

Two results worth remembering: a central point load on a simply supported span gives Mmax​=PL/4, and a uniform load gives Mmax​=qL2/8.

Worked exampleA footbridge span

6 m simply supported, 20 kN at 2 m plus 5 kN/m along the whole span.

  1. Reactions: Rb​=(20⋅2+30⋅3)/6=21.667 kN, Ra​=50−21.667=28.333 kN.
  2. Shear just left of the point load: 28.333−5⋅2=18.333 kN. Just right: 18.333−20=−1.667 kN. It changes sign at x=2 m.
  3. So Mmax​=M(2)=28.333⋅2−5⋅22/2=46.667 kN m.
  4. Checks in the code: a central 30 kN load on 6 m gives PL/4=45 kN m; 8 kN/m gives qL2/8=36 kN m; numerically dM/dx=V and dV/dx=−q everywhere.

Exercise 1A balcony cantilever

A balcony beam sticks out 1.8 m from a wall. It carries 2 kN/m (deck and people) and a 1.5 kN planter at the tip. Find the shear and moment at the wall.

  1. Take the part to the right of a cut at the wall. Shear: 1.5+2⋅1.8=5.1 kN.
  2. Moment: −(1.5⋅1.8+2⋅1.82/2)=−(2.7+3.24)=−5.94 kN m. It is negative (hogging): the top of the beam is in tension, so a concrete balcony needs its steel near the top.

05.14.title: Cables and chains
05.14.html:
Cable cars, power lines, suspension bridges and washing lines all hang in a curve set by their own weight. Cables can only pull, so they find the one shape in which pure tension balances the load. For self-weight that shape is the catenary, and finding it is a nice combination of statics, calculus and root finding.

The equation of a hanging cable

Take a cable with weight w per unit length. Cut out a piece from the lowest point to x. The horizontal tension H is the same everywhere (no horizontal loads), and the vertical component at x must carry the weight of the piece, ws:

dxdy​=Hws​.

Differentiating, with ds=1+y′2​dx, and solving gives the catenary

y=acoshax​,a=wH​.

The tension at any point is T=wy: it grows by w times the height you climb.

Span, length, sag

For supports at equal height a span S apart, the cable length is L=2asinh(S/2a). Given S and L, that equation has no closed-form solution for a, but the left side falls steadily as a grows, so bisection finds it reliably. Then the sag is d=a(cosh(S/2a)−1).

When the sag is small, the catenary is very close to a parabola (the exact shape for a load spread evenly along the span, as on a suspension bridge deck):

H≈8dwS2​,L≈S+3S8d2​.

Note how tension grows as sag falls. A perfectly straight cable would need infinite tension, which is why power lines always sag.

Worked exampleA cable-car track rope

Span 400 m, rope 404 m, 30 kg/m (w=0.2943 kN/m).

  1. Bisection on 2asinh(200/a)=404: a=817.7 m.
  2. Sag d=817.7(cosh(200/817.7)−1)=24.58 m.
  3. H=wa=240.65 kN; at the towers T=H+wd=247.89 kN.
  4. The parabola gives a sag of 24.50 m and H=240.29 kN, within 0.4 %.
  5. A slack 14 m chain on a 10 m span sags 4.38 m, but the parabola says 3.87 m. The code also checks that the arc-length integral returns the specified length.

Exercise 1A power line

A power line weighs 15 N/m and spans 250 m between towers of equal height. The design limit for horizontal tension is 20 kN. Using the parabolic approximation, what is the minimum sag, and how much longer than the span is the conductor?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. d=wS2/(8H)=15⋅2502/(8⋅20000)=5.86 m.
  2. L−S≈8d2/(3S)=8⋅5.862/750=0.366 m. Only 37 cm of extra conductor makes almost 6 m of sag.
  3. On a hot day the conductor expands, L grows, and the sag increases noticeably. That’s why clearance is checked at maximum temperature.

05.15.title: Friction
05.15.html:
Friction is why ladders stand, bolts stay tight and crates stay put on a truck ramp, until they don’t. The model engineers use for dry contact is two centuries old and fits on one line. It’s an approximation, but used carefully it predicts whether something will slide, tip or hold.

Coulomb friction

At a dry contact with normal force N, the friction force F adjusts itself to whatever equilibrium needs, up to a limit:

∣F∣≤μs​N(sticking),∣F∣=μk​N(sliding).

μs​ (static) is usually a little larger than μk​ (kinetic). Typical values: rubber on dry asphalt 0.7 to 0.9, steel on steel 0.5 to 0.8 dry and around 0.1 lubricated, wood on wood 0.3 to 0.5. They are measured, not derived, and vary a lot.

Two things to remember:

  • Friction is not automatically μN. It is μN only at the point of slipping. Otherwise it is whatever the FBD needs.
  • The friction force is independent of the contact area (to a first approximation).

Slide or tip

A crate of width b and height h on a ramp at angle θ:

  • Slides when the friction needed, Wsinθ, exceeds μWcosθ, i.e. when tanθ>μ. The weight doesn’t matter.
  • Tips when the weight’s line of action passes outside the lower edge, i.e. when tanθ>b/h.

Whichever limit is smaller happens first as the ramp tilts. A tall, narrow crate on a grippy ramp tips; a squat one on a slippery ramp slides. The same reasoning applies to pushing a crate: push high and it tips, push low and it slides.

Worked exampleA fridge on a truck ramp

Crate 0.6 m wide, 1.2 m tall: b/h=0.5, so it would tip at arctan0.5=26.57°.

  1. On a smooth steel ramp, μ=0.3: arctan0.3=16.70°<26.57°. It slides first, at 16.70°.
  2. On a rubber mat, μ=0.6: 26.57°<arctan0.6=30.96°. It tips first, at 26.57°. Strap it.
  3. Pushing it across the floor (900 N, μ=0.4): sliding needs 360 N. Tipping about the front edge needs 900⋅0.3/hp​, which is less than 360 N once hp​>0.75 m. Push below 0.75 m.

Exercise 1A wedge under a door

A door pushes horizontally on a thin wooden wedge with 40 N. The wedge angle is 8° and μ=0.35 on both faces. Does the wedge hold? Ignore the wedge’s weight.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Use the friction angle φ=arctanμ=arctan0.35=19.29°. At each face the total contact force can tilt up to φ from the normal.
  2. A wedge of angle α with friction on both faces stays put (is self-locking) when α<2φ: the two contact forces can then line up and cancel. Here 8°<38.6°, so it holds with a large margin.
  3. The 40 N doesn’t matter for whether it holds: both the push-out tendency and the friction scale with it. That’s what makes a wedge self-locking.

05.16.title: Belt friction
05.16.html:
A deckhand stops a drifting ship by wrapping a rope a few times round a bollard and holding the free end with one hand. Climbers lower each other with a rope round a friction device; belts drive alternators and pumps. All of this rests on one striking result: friction on a curved surface grows exponentially with the wrap angle.

The Euler–Eytelwein formula

Take a rope wrapped round a fixed drum, about to slip, with tension T1​ on the slack side and T2​ on the tight side. Look at a short piece spanning angle dθ:

  • the two end tensions, T and T+dT, are tangent to the drum;
  • radially they press the rope on with dN=Tdθ;
  • at the point of slipping, friction μdN makes up the difference: dT=μTdθ.

Integrate over the wrap angle β (in radians):

TdT​=μdθ⟹T1​T2​​=eμβ.

The drum’s radius drops out. With μ=0.3, one turn gives a ratio of 6.6, two turns 43, three turns 286. Each extra turn multiplies by the same factor.

Belt drives and V-belts

A belt transmits torque (T1​−T2​)r through the friction on its pulley, and slips when T1​/T2​ reaches eμβ on the pulley with the smaller wrap. A V-belt wedges into its groove, which multiplies the normal force: with groove angle 2α the effective friction coefficient is μ/sinα, about three times larger for a 40° groove.

Worked exampleA bollard and a belt drive

  1. Three turns (β=6π) with μ=0.3: T2​/T1​=e5.655=285.7.

05.17.title: Centres of mass and gravity
05.17.html:
Weight is spread through a body, but for statics you can treat it as one force at the centre of gravity. Where that point sits decides whether a crane tips, how a beam section bends (its centroid is where bending stress is zero) and how a bike handles. This lesson shows how to find it for composite shapes, checks the result against a general polygon formula, and adds a neat shortcut for volumes of revolution.

Definitions

For a body of mass m, the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position:

rˉ=m1​∫rdm.

In a uniform gravity field it is also the centre of gravity. For a flat shape of uniform thickness, it is the centroid of the area: xˉ=A1​∫xdA, and similarly for yˉ​. A symmetry axis always contains the centroid.

Composite shapes

Most engineering shapes are built from rectangles, triangles and circles. Use the known centroid of each part and take the weighted average:

xˉ=∑Ai​∑Ai​xˉi​​,yˉ​=∑Ai​∑Ai​yˉ​i​​.

A hole is a part with negative area. For any polygon, the shoelace formula gives the same answer straight from the vertices, which makes a good cross-check:

A=21​∑(xi​yi+1​−xi+1​yi​),xˉ=6A1​∑(xi​+xi+1​)(xi​yi+1​−xi+1​yi​).

Pappus–Guldinus

Revolve a plane area A about an axis in its plane that doesn’t cut it. The volume swept is the area times the distance its centroid travels:

V=2πrˉA.

The same holds for surface areas swept by a curve. It turns tyre, O-ring and pipe-bend volumes into one-line calculations.

Worked exampleA T-section and an L-bracket

  1. T-section: flange 200 × 30 mm on a 30 × 170 mm web. Areas 6000 and 5100 mm², centroids at 185 and 85 mm. yˉ​=(6000⋅185+5100⋅85)/11100=139.05 mm above the bottom. The polygon formula on the 8 vertices gives the same.
  2. L-bracket: 100 × 10 base plus 10 × 70 upright on its left end. xˉ=(1000⋅50+700⋅5)/1700=31.47 mm, yˉ​=(1000⋅5+700⋅45)/1700=21.47 mm.
  3. A 300 × 200 plate with an 80 mm hole centred at x=220 mm: xˉ=(60000⋅150−5026.5⋅220)/54973.5=143.60 mm. It moves away from the hole.
  4. Pappus: a cone made by revolving a right triangle (base 0.5 m, height 1.2 m) has V=2π⋅(0.5/3)⋅0.3=0.3142 m³ =πr2h/3.

Exercise 1An inner-tube volume

A bicycle inner tube is roughly a torus: tube radius 20 mm, centre-line radius 330 mm. Find its volume with Pappus.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The revolved area is a circle: A=π⋅0.022=1.257×10−3 m², centroid at rˉ=0.33 m.
  2. V=2π⋅0.33⋅1.257×10−3=2.606×10−3 m³, about 2.6 litres.

05.18.title: Hydrostatics
05.18.html:
Switzerland stores a large share of its electricity as water behind alpine dams. The force that water puts on a dam wall or a gate follows from statics alone, because still water can’t carry shear: it only pushes, perpendicular to every surface, with a pressure that grows with depth. This lesson computes the force on submerged plane surfaces and where it acts.

Pressure in still water

Take a small vertical column of water. Its weight must be carried by the pressure difference between its bottom and top, so

dzdp​=−ρg⟹p=ρgh,

where h is the depth below the free surface (gauge pressure, ignoring the air above). At 50 m that’s about 490 kPa, nearly five atmospheres. Pressure at a point is the same in every direction.

Force on a plane surface

For a flat gate of area A, the total force is the integral of the pressure, which comes out as the pressure at the centroid times the area:

F=∫pdA=ρghc​A.

It doesn’t act at the centroid, though. Pressure is larger lower down, so the centre of pressure sits below the centroid. Measured along the plane of the gate (slant distance s from the surface line),

scp​=sc​+sc​AIc​​,

with Ic​ the second moment of area of the gate about its own horizontal centroidal axis (bL3/12 for a rectangle). For a vertical rectangle reaching up to the surface, this gives the classic result: F=ρgbh2/2, acting at 2h/3 below the surface. For a deep gate, Ic​/(sc​A) is tiny and the centre of pressure almost coincides with the centroid.

Worked exampleGates and a dam

  1. Vertical gate, 3 m wide, from the surface to 4 m deep: F=1000⋅9.81⋅3⋅42/2=235.4 kN at 2⋅4/3=2.667 m depth.
  2. Bottom outlet gate, 2 m wide and 3 m tall, centred 50 m deep: F=1000⋅9.81⋅50⋅6=2.943 MN. Ic​=2⋅33/12=4.5 m⁴, so the centre of pressure is 4.5/(50⋅6)=0.015 m below the centroid.
  3. Inclined gate at 60°, 2 m wide, slant length 5 m from the surface: F=1000⋅9.81⋅(2.5sin60°)⋅10=212.4 kN at slant distance 3.333 m.
  4. A 60 m deep reservoir pushes ρgh2/2=17.66 MN on each metre of dam, 20 m above the base: an overturning moment of 353 MN m per metre that the dam’s weight must resist. The code checks each closed form by integrating the pressure.

Exercise 1A sluice gate

A vertical sluice gate 1.5 m wide and 2 m tall has its top edge 1 m below the water surface. Find the force and the depth of the centre of pressure.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Centroid depth hc​=1+1=2 m, area 3 m². F=1000⋅9.81⋅2⋅3=58.86 kN.
  2. Ic​=1.5⋅23/12=1 m⁴. scp​=2+1/(2⋅3)=2.167 m deep.
  3. The hinge or seal design uses this point: a hinge placed exactly at the centre of pressure would leave the gate balanced.

05.19.title: The principle of virtual work
05.19.html:
A scissor lift has nine unknown pin forces. You could draw three free-body diagrams and solve nine equations, or you could use one equation that never mentions a pin force at all. The principle of virtual work replaces force balance with a work balance, and for mechanisms with one degree of freedom it is often the fastest route to the answer.

The principle

Imagine giving a body in equilibrium a tiny, imaginary displacement that its supports allow: a virtual displacement δr. Since the resultant force and moment are zero, the total work they do is zero too:

δW=i∑​Fi​⋅δri​=0for every admissible virtual displacement.

The useful part: ideal constraints (smooth pins, rollers, rigid links) do no work in such a displacement. Their reactions drop out. For a mechanism with one degree of freedom θ, write every loaded point’s position as a function of θ, differentiate, and the equilibrium condition becomes one scalar equation.

The recipe

  1. Choose one coordinate θ that describes the mechanism’s position.
  2. Write the position of each point where an active force acts: yW​(θ), xP​(θ), and so on.
  3. Differentiate: δyW​=yW′​(θ)δθ.
  4. Set ∑Fδ(position)=0 and solve for the unknown force.

It’s the same idea as mechanical advantage (05.12): output force times output motion equals input force times input motion.

Worked exampleA scissor lift

One stage, links of length L at angle θ, load W=4 kN on the platform. The actuator spans the base ends, x=Lcosθ; the platform is at y=Lsinθ.

  1. Virtual displacement: δy=Lcosθδθ, δx=−Lsinθδθ.
  2. The load does work −Wδy; the actuator, pushing the ends together, does −Pδx.
  3. −WLcosθδθ+PLsinθδθ=0, so P=Wcotθ. With n stages, y=nLsinθ and P=nWcotθ.
  4. At 35°: P=4cot35°=5.713 kN. At 20°: 10.99 kN. At 60°: 2.309 kN.
  5. The code solves the full nine-unknown FBD system (two links, platform, every pin) and gets the same numbers.

Exercise 1A three-stage lift

A three-stage scissor lift carries 4 kN. What actuator force does it need at 20°, and at what angle does the force drop to 4 kN?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. P=3⋅4cot20°=12⋅2.747=32.97 kN.
  2. P=4 kN when cotθ=4/12=1/3, so θ=arctan3=71.57°.
  3. This is why real lifts mount the actuator diagonally rather than horizontally: it improves the leverage when folded.

05.20.title: Stability of equilibrium
05.20.html:
A pencil balanced on its tip is in equilibrium: forces and moments balance. So is a pencil lying on the table. Only one of them stays that way when someone breathes on it. Statics so far asked whether a position is in equilibrium; this last lesson asks whether it stays there. The answer comes from potential energy, and it’s the doorway to buckling in Phase 06.

Energy and equilibrium

For a conservative system (weights and springs), the total potential energy V(θ) depends on the position coordinate θ. The virtual work principle (05.19) says equilibrium is where a small displacement does no work, which is where the energy is stationary:

dθdV​=0.

Its stability depends on the second derivative:

dθ2d2V​>0stable (a valley),<0unstable (a hilltop),=0neutral (test higher derivatives).

A small push into a valley raises the energy, so the system has to be pushed back. A ball on a landscape is the picture to keep in mind.

An inverted bar with a spring

A rigid bar of length L stands upright on a hinge with a rotational spring of stiffness k, carrying a load P on top. Leaning it by θ stores spring energy and lowers the load:

V(θ)=21​kθ2+PLcosθ,V′(θ)=kθ−PLsinθ,V′′(θ)=k−PLcosθ.

θ=0 is always an equilibrium, and it is stable if V′′(0)=k−PL>0, i.e. for

P<Pcr​=Lk​.

Above the critical load, upright is unstable and the bar leans over to a new stable equilibrium where kθ=PLsinθ. That is buckling in its simplest form: a structure that was fine under a smaller load suddenly finds a lower-energy position sideways.

Worked exampleBelow and above the critical load

k=20 kN m/rad, L=2 m, so Pcr​=10 kN.

  1. P=8 kN: V′′(0)=20−16=4>0. Upright is stable.
  2. P=12 kN: V′′(0)=20−24=−4<0. Upright is unstable.
  3. Solving 20θ=24sinθ by bisection gives θ=±58.83°, where V′′=20−24cos58.83°=7.58>0: stable leaning positions.
  4. The code checks each second derivative against finite differences, and checks that a small push raises the energy exactly when V′′>0.

Exercise 1A horizontal spring instead

Replace the rotational spring by a horizontal spring of stiffness k=5 kN/m at the top of the 2 m bar, which stays horizontal as the bar leans. Then V=21​k(Lsinθ)2+PLcosθ. Find Pcr​, and classify the leaning equilibria for P=8 kN.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. V′=Lsinθ(kLcosθ−P) and V′′(0)=kL2−PL, so Pcr​=kL=10 kN.
  2. For P=8 kN, besides θ=0 (stable), there are equilibria where cosθ=P/(kL)=0.8, i.e. θ=±36.87°.
  3. There V′′=−kL2sin2θ=−5⋅4⋅0.36=−7.2<0: unstable. These hilltops are the edges of the valley. Push the bar past 36.87° and it falls over, even though the load is below the critical value. Structures like this are sensitive to imperfections, a theme Phase 06 picks up with real columns.
